notes: The natural quantity would be the optimal stability exponent alpha, but no bound on either side is known; Baek gives only optimality. This is a qualitative/stability problem, not a bound problem.
title: Sofa stability
W: Baek (2024) proved that Gerver's sofa has the largest area among shapes that can be moved around a right-angled corner in a hallway of width 1. Show that any movable sofa whose area is nearly Gerver's must be nearly Gerver's sofa in shape (which in particular gives uniqueness).
M: A moving sofa is a compact connected $S\subset\mathbb R^2$ that can be moved by a continuous rigid motion from $(-\infty,0]\times[0,1]$ to $[0,1]\times(-\infty,0]$ inside $L=((-\infty,1]\times[0,1])\cup([0,1]\times(-\infty,1])$. Let $G$ be Gerver's sofa, of area $A_G\approx2.21953$. Prove that there are $C,\alpha>0$ such that every moving sofa $S$ with $|S|\ge A_G-\varepsilon$ satisfies $\min_{g}|gS\,\triangle\,G|\le C\varepsilon^{\alpha}$, the minimum over rigid motions $g$ of the plane.
why: Baek's proof gives optimality, but its abstract claims neither uniqueness nor stability. A quantitative stability inequality is the standard sharpening of an isoperimetric-type theorem, as for Bonnesen-type and Fusco-Maggi-Pratelli results, and would make the solution robust, for example for numerical verification.

title: Critical linear firefighter rate on Z^3
quantity: c* = inf{c: floor(ct) firefighters at step t contain every finite outbreak on Z^3}
lower: c* >= 8/243 (~0.033), elementary: Loomis-Whitney gives |vertex boundary of B| >= |B|^{2/3}; for c<2a^2-6a^3 with a=2/9, a large initial cube burns forever by induction b_t >= (a(t+T0))^3. Using the asymptotically sharp Wang-Wang vertex isoperimetry (l1-balls, constant 4(3/4)^{2/3}) the same argument heuristically gives ~32/27, not checked rigorously
upper: c* <= 8, elementary: protect the l1-sphere |x|_1=D (4D^2+2 vertices) before step D-R; c>8 suffices for large D. Finiteness was known (Dyer-Martinez-Pedroza-Thorne, arXiv:1507.03050, Cor. 4, constant not explicit); o(t) fails (arXiv:2002.11205)
W: On the 3D grid, a finite fire spreads to all unprotected neighbours each step, and at step t you may protect about ct new vertices. It is known that linear growth is the right order. Elementary arguments show that rate c>8 always contains the fire and that c<8/243 does not. Narrow this gap, or find the exact critical rate.
M: Firefighter game on $\mathbb Z^3$: a finite $X_0$ burns at time 0; at step $t\ge1$ first protect $\lfloor ct\rfloor$ unburnt vertices (permanently), then fire spreads to all unprotected neighbours of burning vertices. Let $c^*=\inf\{c>0:$ for every finite $X_0$ the fire is contained$\}$. Known: $8/243\le c^*\le 8$ (elementary isoperimetric and l1-sphere wall arguments). Improve either bound; e.g. prove $c^*<8$ by a strategy that beats a static wall, or $c^*\ge 1$.
why: This is the 3D analogue of the Z^2 question of how many firefighters per turn contain any finite outbreak (Fogarty: 2 suffice; Feldheim-Hod: 3/2 do not suffice in general). The order t^{d-2} is settled, but no constant has been studied. The lower bound is pure isoperimetry, and beating the static l1-wall would show that dynamic blocking helps.
notes: Both bounds derived by me (proof sketches in the lower/upper fields; discrete recursion checked numerically). No literature constant found. Fogarty/Feldheim-Hod Z^2 facts from memory, not re-verified.
The bound quantity liminf d(n)/p(n) is the problem itself. No nontrivial proven lower bound was found, and arXiv:2410.01726 already poses it, so a bound version adds nothing.
title: Distinct character degrees of the symmetric group
W: Conjugate partitions always give representations of S_n of the same dimension, so at most about half of the p(n) irreducible representations can have distinct dimensions. Decide whether the fraction of distinct dimensions tends to a limit, and whether that limit is positive.
M: Let $d(n)=\#\{f^\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ be the number of distinct irreducible character degrees of $S_n$, so $d(n)\le (p(n)+sc(n))/2$, where $sc(n)$ is the number of self-conjugate partitions. Determine whether $\lim_{n\to\infty}d(n)/p(n)$ exists and, if so, find it; in particular decide whether $\liminf_n d(n)/p(n)>0$. (Hook-length data: $d(n)/p(n)\in[0.40,0.47]$ for $20\le n\le45$, e.g. $d(40)=16216$, $p(40)=37338$; computations up to $n=129$ in arXiv:2410.01726 show the average multiplicity $p(n)/d(n)$ with no clear limit, possibly near $2.5$.)
why: Degrees of S_n are products of hook lengths, and coincidences between them beyond conjugation are a basic but poorly understood arithmetic phenomenon. Whether the average degree multiplicity stays bounded says how much of the information in a partition is lost in its dimension.

notes: Grade C. No bound quantity. Haslhofer-Ketover (arXiv:2307.01828) give >=3 disks in convex balls, sharp generically, but B_4 already has 9 planar ones. The nonplanar disk looks routine (IFT near p=2). No honest C_TO_B fix verified.
title: Non-flat free-boundary minimal disks in the superball
W: In a round ball the only free-boundary minimal disks are flat slices through the centre (Nitsche). The superball x^4+y^4+z^4 <= 1 has nine flat ones, cut by its mirror planes. Is there also one that is not flat? A natural candidate has threefold symmetry about the diagonal (1,1,1).
M: For $p>2$ let $B_p=\{|x|^p+|y|^p+|z|^p\le1\}$. Decide whether $B_4$ (more generally $B_p$) contains an embedded minimal disk $\Sigma$ with $\partial\Sigma\subset\partial B_p$, meeting $\partial B_p$ orthogonally, that is not contained in a plane. Specifically, show that there is one invariant under the rotation by $2\pi/3$ about the axis $\mathbb R(1,1,1)$ and under $v\mapsto-v$.
why: Nitsche's uniqueness theorem for the round ball, together with min-max existence results for free-boundary minimal disks in convex bodies, raises the question of how many such disks a convex body has and of what kind. The superball is the simplest symmetric convex body where the answer is not forced by planes of symmetry.

notes: Non-integrability is qualitative; there is no natural bound quantity.
title: Three identical vortices on a square torus are chaotic
W: On a flat torus, three point vortices with total circulation zero form an integrable system (Stremler-Aref), but for vortices of equal strength even three are believed chaotic, from numerics only. Prove that three identical point vortices on the square torus are not integrable; the same question is open for four.
M: Let $G$ be the Green function of $\mathbb T=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)$ ($\Delta G=\delta_0-1$) and $H=-\sum_{i<j}G(z_i-z_j)$ on $\{(z_1,\dots,z_N)\in\mathbb T^N: z_i\ne z_j\}$ with symplectic form $\sum_i dx_i\wedge dy_i$. The centre $Z=\sum_i z_i\in\mathbb T$ is conserved; the reduced space $M_N=\{Z=Z_0\}/(\tfrac1N\mathbb Z[i]/\mathbb Z[i])$ is symplectic of dimension $2N-2$. Prove that for $N=3$ the reduced flow on $M_3$ has no real-analytic first integral functionally independent of $H$ (and likewise for $N=4$ on $M_4$).
why: Point-vortex systems are the standard finite-dimensional models of 2D Euler; integrability is classified on the plane, sphere and for zero total circulation on the torus, but for nonzero circulation on the torus the translation momenta do not commute and only N=2 is integrable. Proving non-integrability for N=3 identical vortices would be the first rigorous chaos result for vortex lattices, where only numerics (Borisov-Mamaev-Kilin) exist.

notes: Grade C. Numerically easy and affirmative. The only quantity, the spectral gap scaling with n, is artificial. No honest fix to solid B.
title: Frozen vortices for Kuramoto on a cube
W: Identical Kuramoto oscillators sit on the grid of a cube's surface. Besides full synchrony, there is a 'longitude' state with a vortex at the centre of the top face and an antivortex at the centre of the bottom face. Prove that this state is a linearly stable equilibrium for every grid size.
M: Let $Q_n$ be the vertex–edge graph of the $n\times n$ subdivided surface of the cube, and $\dot\theta_i=\sum_{j\sim i}\sin(\theta_j-\theta_i)$. Prove that for every odd $n\ge3$ there is an equilibrium $\theta^*$ with the cube's 4-fold rotational symmetry about the vertical axis and winding number $\pm1$ around the central plaquettes of the top and bottom faces, whose Jacobian (the Laplacian with edge weights $\cos(\theta^*_j-\theta^*_i)$) has kernel exactly $\mathrm{span}(\mathbf 1)$ and is otherwise positive. (More generally: for which $n$ does $Q_n$ have a stable non-synchronous equilibrium?)
why: On graphs that triangulate or quadrangulate a sphere there are no twisted states, so any stable non-synchronous state must come from discrete vortices pinned by the lattice. Most known stability criteria need every phase difference below π/2, and this state violates that: by symmetry the central-plaquette edges sit at exactly π/2. So it is a small test case for stability beyond that regime.

notes: Proof-size question. Its bounds are qualitative (poly vs exp), and no current best bounds are known to state. Stays as is.
title: Proof complexity of the sensitivity theorem
W: Huang proved that any set of more than half the corners of the n-cube contains a corner with at least √n neighbours inside the set. Write this as a propositional formula with one variable per corner. Do polynomial-size proofs exist in resolution, cutting planes or sum-of-squares, measured against the 2^n variables?
M: Let $N=2^n$, $d=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil-1$. $\mathrm{SENS}_n$ is the CNF on variables $x_v$ ($v\in\{0,1\}^n$) plus sequential-counter variables encoding $\sum_v x_v\ge 2^{n-1}+1$, together with the clauses $\neg x_v\vee\bigvee_{u\in U}\neg x_u$ for every $v$ and every $(d+1)$-set $U$ of neighbours of $v$ (size $N\cdot n^{O(\sqrt n)}=N^{1+o(1)}$). It is unsatisfiable by Huang's theorem. Does $\mathrm{SENS}_n$ have refutations of size $N^{O(1)}$ in (a) resolution, (b) cutting planes, (c) sum-of-squares of degree $O(\log N)$? Lower bounds $2^{N^{\Omega(1)}}$ are equally of interest.
why: Huang's proof is a short spectral argument, interlacing for a signed adjacency matrix. Asking whether weak proof systems can capture it tests how much linear algebra cutting planes and SOS can simulate. It belongs to the programme of locating famous combinatorial theorems in the proof-complexity hierarchy.

notes: Decidability question; there is no quantity.
title: Deciding rationality of PL rotation numbers
W: A circle homeomorphism made of finitely many straight pieces, with rational break points and slopes, has a rotation number. Rational rotation numbers can be confirmed by finding a rational periodic orbit. Irrational ones occur too: Belk–Hyde–Moore found √2−1 with slopes 3/2, 2/3, 1. Is there an algorithm that always decides which case holds?
M: Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of orientation-preserving PL homeomorphisms of $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with finitely many rational break points, rational slopes and $f(0)\in\mathbb Q$, encoded by these data. Is $\{f\in\mathcal P:\rho(f)\in\mathbb Q\}$ decidable? (It is computably enumerable: if $\rho(f)=p/q$, the zero set of the lift $F^q(x)-x-p$ is a nonempty finite union of rational points and rational intervals.)
why: Rotation numbers of rational PL maps link Thompson-like groups $T_q$, renormalisation, and number theory. Belk–Hyde–Moore conjecture that the irrational values are quadratic when slopes are powers of one rational, and they ask about decidability for one-parameter families and for finite order in $T_q$. A decision procedure would amount to a structure theorem for when renormalisation of such maps fails to close up.

notes: Grade C. Routine adaptation of Merle; no quantity. Switching to the Ablowitz-Musslimani u^2 conj(u(-x)) nonlinearity could be a fix, but I could not verify its status, so it stays C.
title: Minimal-mass blow-up with reflection
W: Consider the 2D Schrödinger equation in which the self-interaction at each point uses the density at the mirror point -x. Below the ground-state mass, solutions exist forever. Show that the only solutions that blow up with exactly the ground-state mass are the explicit pseudo-conformal ground-state solutions centred at the origin.
M: Let $Q>0$ be the radial solution of $\Delta Q-Q+Q^3=0$ on $\mathbb R^2$. Consider $iu_t+\Delta u+|u(-x,t)|^2u=0$ with $u_0\in H^1(\mathbb R^2)$ and $\|u_0\|_{L^2}=\|Q\|_{L^2}$. Prove that if $u$ blows up at a finite time $T$, then there are $\theta\in\mathbb R$ and $\lambda>0$ with $u(t,x)=e^{i\theta}\frac{\lambda}{T-t}\,Q\!\Big(\frac{\lambda x}{T-t}\Big)\exp\!\Big(i\frac{\lambda^2}{T-t}-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}\Big)$.
why: Merle's classification of minimal-mass blow-up for the focusing mass-critical NLS is a model rigidity theorem. The reflection nonlinearity breaks translation and Galilean invariance but keeps scaling and the pseudo-conformal symmetry about the origin. It is therefore a simple test of which symmetries the rigidity argument actually needs.

notes: Liouville rigidity is qualitative; there is no bound quantity.
title: A Jörgens theorem for the Hessian permanent
W: Jörgens proved that a convex function on the whole plane whose Hessian determinant is 1 must be a quadratic polynomial. Replace the determinant by the permanent, u_xx·u_yy + u_xy², and ask whether the same rigidity holds for solutions on the elliptic branch.
M: Let $u\in C^4(\mathbb R^2)$ satisfy $u_{xx}u_{yy}+u_{xy}^2=1$, $u_{xx}>0$ and $2u_{xy}^2<1$ on $\mathbb R^2$ (these are exactly the conditions for the linearized operator $u_{yy}\partial_{xx}+2u_{xy}\partial_{xy}+u_{xx}\partial_{yy}$ to be elliptic; they force $u$ convex with $0<\det D^2u=1-2u_{xy}^2\le1$). Prove or disprove that $u$ is a quadratic polynomial.
why: Jörgens' theorem and its extensions (Calabi, Pogorelov; Yuan's work on special Lagrangian equations) depend on the Monge–Ampère or Lagrangian structure, which allows Lewy or Legendre-type transformations to linear or holomorphic problems. The permanent level set {ac+b²=1} is a one-sheeted hyperboloid. It is not a symplectic Monge–Ampère equation, its ellipticity degenerates both at infinity and at the finite boundary 2b²=1, and in two dimensions Liouville theorems are known in general only for uniformly elliptic F (Nirenberg). So this is a clean test of whether 2D Bernstein–Jörgens rigidity needs the special structure.
